cards.b: A large rotating storm with low pressure, winds over 119 km/h, heavy rain and storm surge, forming over warm tropical oceans.
Same storm, different places: hurricane (Atlantic/NE Pacific), typhoon (NW Pacific), cyclone (Indian Ocean/South Pacific).
Over warm oceans between about 5° and 30° north and south of the equator.
At least 27°C, to a depth of about 50 metres.
The Coriolis force is too weak there to make the air spin.
The effect of the Earth's rotation that makes moving air spin: anticlockwise in the north, clockwise in the south.
A change in wind speed or direction with height. High shear tears a developing storm apart, so low shear is needed.
The calm centre with sinking air, clear skies and light winds, surrounded by the eyewall with the strongest winds.

cards.f: Why does a cyclone weaken over land?
cards.b: It loses its supply of warm moist air (energy), and friction slows the wind.
Categories 1–5 based on sustained wind speed. Category 1 begins at 74 mph; Category 5 is 157 mph or more.
A rise in sea level caused by low pressure and strong winds; it floods low coasts and causes most deaths.
Immediate: buildings destroyed, trees and power lines down, flooding, deaths and injuries.
Later: disease from dirty water, food shortages, homelessness, lost jobs, landslides, economic damage.

cards.f: Why are poorer countries more vulnerable?
cards.b: Weak housing, exposed locations, poor roads and warnings, less money for defences, shelters and recovery.
Satellites, radar, aircraft and storm tracking show the path and strength, giving days of warning.
Warnings, evacuation, cyclone shelters, stronger buildings, storm shutters, sea walls and hazard maps.
Search and rescue, emergency food, water and medicine, temporary shelter and international aid.
Rebuilding to higher standards, hazard mapping, risk assessment, improved defences and economic recovery.

short.q: Explain why wind shear must be low for a tropical cyclone to form.
short.model: High wind shear tears apart the tall column of rising air and clouds, so the storm cannot organise or intensify.
points: high shear disrupts/tears apart the storm
low shear lets the rising column build

short.q: Describe one way that storm tracking helps reduce deaths.
short.model: Satellites and radar show the path and strength of the storm, so authorities can warn people and evacuate them from areas likely to be hit.

short.q: Give two reasons why a tropical cyclone may cause fewer deaths in a richer country.
short.model: There is better warning and evacuation using good roads and communication, and stronger buildings and defences that survive the winds and surge.

short.q: Explain how a storm surge is produced by a tropical cyclone.
short.model: Very low pressure at the centre lets the sea rise up, and strong winds push the water towards the coast, causing flooding when it reaches low land.
points: low pressure lets sea level rise
winds push water onto the coast, flooding

short.q: Explain one long-term response to a tropical cyclone.
short.model: Rebuilding homes and infrastructure to higher standards, and drawing up hazard maps so that new building avoids flood-risk zones.
